title: Arithmetic: complete groups, a remainder and safe calculations
goal: Choose division and remainder to fit the task, trace compound assignments, and check the range before calculating.

prerequisites.text: Named values, type ranges, and expression grouping.
Simple if and early return from Module 1 are repeated in a protective scaffold. Full logic is treated in lesson 9.

sections.title: Why −7 / 3 gives −2
paragraphs: Seven items fill two boxes of three with one item left. But what does −7 / 3 mean? The picture of physical boxes is no longer enough; we need the language rule.
Predict the quotient and remainder, then check the relationship dividend = quotient × divisor + remainder. It reveals the sign of the remainder without memorising each case separately.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and follow the steps
paragraphs: For integers, 7 / 3 is 2. −7 / 3 is −2: the fraction is discarded toward zero rather than rounded down to −3. −7 % 3 is −1 because −7 = (−2) × 3 + (−1). A nonzero remainder has the dividend’s sign, not necessarily the divisor’s.

Check 7 / −3 and −7 / −3 with the same identity. This is not the always-nonnegative mathematical modulo used in some tasks. Do not assume % produces an index in 0…b−1 for negative inputs. Here we explain the result; range normalization belongs to a later concrete task.
Change only the divisor’s sign: −7 / −3 gives 2 and the remainder stays −1. Check −7 = 2 × (−3) − 1. A remainder is not necessarily positive.

sections.title: Reject invalid division before evaluating it
paragraphs: For integers a zero divisor is invalid for both / and %. Another dangerous boundary is the minimum signed value divided by −1 when the quotient is unrepresentable. A successful build does not make these runtime operations valid. We do not execute them for an error screenshot.

The laboratory scaffold checks invalid bounds before dividing. || means or: if any rejection condition is true, it prints invalid and return 0 ends processing. This repeats the protective scaffold from Module 1 rather than requiring new independent branching design.

sections.title: Tracing +=, -= and *=
paragraphs: For a simple int stock, stock += 4; adds 4, stock -= 3; subtracts 3, and stock *= 2; doubles it. The sequence is 10 → 14 → 11 → 22. /= and %= replace the value with the quotient and remainder. Division and range restrictions still apply.

For a simple name, x += y updates x with the sum. Do not generalize this to a blind textual rewrite of complex left expressions: compound assignment evaluates its left operand once. We use ordinary names only, without arrays, pointers, or effectful functions.

sections.title: Choose the wider type before multiplying
paragraphs: Let width and height be ints equal to 50000. In long long area = width * height;, the product is evaluated as int when both operands remain int. On a target with 32-bit int, 2500000000 does not fit. The wider area destination cannot help. We discuss this unsafe form without executing it.

In the safe example 1LL is a long long literal with value 1. 1LL * width * height starts multiplication in a wide integer type. These small nonnegative operands convert safely. Another solution is to declare both operands long long initially. General promotions and conversions follow next; the essential point is widening before the dangerous step.

sections.title: Complete blocks are not enough for a remainder
paragraphs: With bytes=1001 and blockBytes=1000 the quotient is 1 and remainder 1: one full block, but two are needed for storage. For bytes ≥ 0 and blockBytes > 0, (bytes + blockBytes - 1) / blockBytes rounds upward. Zero volume needs zero blocks and an exact multiple needs no extra block.

The formula is not automatically safe near a type maximum: the addition can overflow. We bound bytes to 1000000000000 and blockBytes to 4096, so the numerator is at most 1000000004095 and fits long long. Bounds are checked first. A different contract requires a new proof or another formula.

sections.title: Testing a block boundary
paragraphs: For a block size of 1000, test volumes 0, 999, 1000, and 1001. They distinguish empty volume, remainder, an exact multiple, and the next block. Also test blockBytes=0: expect invalid without executing division.

Record the maximum intermediate bound as well as output. A sanitizer helps find defects in tests, but a few clean runs do not replace reasoning over the stated range. The diagram below traces only the valid example −7 / 3.

sections.title: Intentional: % on double
paragraphs: This is a separate faulty program for examining a diagnostic. It does not replace your work. Locate the cause first, then compare the build failure with a corrected version.
% here requires integer operands. Do not guess a cast that changes the task meaning.

deep.title: Can we round up without another large sum?
deep.text: For a nonnegative numerator and positive denominator, take the integer quotient and add 1 only when the remainder is nonzero: bytes / blockBytes + (bytes % blockBytes != 0). The bool comparison becomes 0 or 1 in this sum. This avoids overflowing bytes + blockBytes − 1, but it does not remove the need to validate the inputs.

sections.title: Now solve a different problem
paragraphs: Complete the starter with complete blocks, remaining bytes and required blocks. The protective if already precedes division; explain its conditions first. Start with a different volume: 2050 bytes and 1024-byte blocks. Predict complete blocks, remainder and required blocks. Then check 0, 1024 and 1025 bytes; keep the zero-size guard before division.
Open Practice. Its starter and your current source are separate from the worked examples. Write a prediction before running, then explain the result in your own words.

feedback: A nonzero remainder has the dividend’s sign; the dividend is −7.
The integer quotient truncates towards zero rather than rounding to 3.

terms.definition: The result of integer / with the fractional part discarded toward zero.
For valid integer division, related to the quotient by a = (a / b) * b + a % b.
An operation such as stock += 4 that updates the left object using its previous value.
A bound on each expression value before the final result is stored.
A signed arithmetic result outside its representable range; it must not be executed as a normal test.
